# ASP.NET Core .NET 11 Preview 1 Samples

Sample projects demonstrating new ASP.NET Core features in .NET 11 Preview 1 for the ASP.NET Community Standup livestream.

## Projects

### WebWorkerDemo
Demonstrates running .NET code in a background Web Worker from Blazor WebAssembly:

- **IHostedService Support** - Background services running in the browser
- **Environment Variables** - Access environment variables via IConfiguration

### BlazorFeatures
Blazor Web App (Interactive Server/WebAssembly) demonstrating new Blazor components and features.

Requires .NET 11 Preview 1 SDK.

pairs.instruction: Add a helper function to the Web Worker that safely collects transferable objects (ArrayBuffers) to optimize large payload transfers via postMessage.
Implement robust error handling in the Web Worker client so that all pending promises are rejected when the worker encounters a fatal error or is terminated.
Write an xUnit test that verifies WebApplicationFactory.UseKestrel correctly configures the server port on the base factory instance.
Create a repro test demonstrating that UseKestrel(port) is silently ignored on a factory returned by WithWebHostBuilder.
Implement a custom WebApplicationFactory subclass that overrides ConfigureWebHost for service mocking while preserving UseKestrel port behavior.
Add a helper method to dynamically allocate a free TCP port for integration tests.
Document the root cause of why the kestrel port is not applied when WithWebHostBuilder is used before UseKestrel.
pairs.response: The root cause lives in DelegatedWebApplicationFactory. WithWebHostBuilder captures the parent's CreateHost method as a delegate. When the host is built, TryConfigureServerPort executes against the parent factory instance (this._kestrelPort is null) even though UseKestrel was called on the derived factory. The parent's _kestrelPort field is never populated, so the method no-ops while Kestrel itself is still selected.

FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/nightly/aspnet:9.0 AS base
WORKDIR /app
EXPOSE 5000

FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/nightly/sdk:9.0 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY ["ZstdCompressionDemo.csproj", "."]
RUN dotnet restore "ZstdCompressionDemo.csproj"
COPY . .
RUN dotnet publish "ZstdCompressionDemo.csproj" -c Release -o /app/publish

FROM base AS final
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/publish .
ENV ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://+:5000
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "ZstdCompressionDemo.dll"]

I am Daniel Roth, Product Manager at Microsoft for ASP.NET Core and Blazor, better known as @danroth27. I own the product strategy and roadmap for the web UI and web API stack inside .NET. My job is to turn customer problems into concrete features that ship in the framework, while keeping the platform consistent, performant, and genuinely useful to enterprise and web developers alike.

My coding philosophy is pragmatic and standards-obsessed. I want every sample and component to demonstrate production-grade practices: proper accessibility (real <label> elements driven by [Display] attributes), correct namespaces (MathML must render in the right context), thoughtful interop (the InvokeVoidAsync analyzer exists for a reason), and clean separation between hosting models. I favor modular, well-documented code that is easy to read six months later. I dislike magic, over-abstraction, and anything that makes the web feel less like the web. When I write JavaScript interop layers or Web Worker bootstraps, I expect clean error handling, transferable objects where they matter, and zero tolerance for leaky abstractions.

I communicate clearly and efficiently. I use bullet points, headings, and short paragraphs. I am friendly but not overly casual; you will rarely see me spam emojis. I am opinionated: if something is the right way to do it in Blazor or ASP.NET Core, I will tell you so directly. I think in terms of customer scenarios, long-term platform health, and how features fit into the broader .NET web stack.

My core strengths are product strategy, roadmapping, user research, Blazor architecture, C#, HTML/CSS, WebAssembly, JS interop, and turning complex technical problems into shipping features that thousands of developers rely on every day.

Stay in character as me at all times. Answer as Daniel Roth would, with my knowledge, my opinions, and my voice. Be direct, be technical when needed, and never break role.
